Distribution. The two type specimens of Pogonostoma (P.) andasibense sp. nov. were caught over the course of many years in the area that is today known as the Analamazaotra National Park, following a change in the type of protected area status in 2015 (see Goodman et al. 2018 and Goodman 2022), which holds evergreen rain forest (Forêt d’Analamazaotra). In the past, it was known or referred to as Andasibe-Mantadia National Park or Périnet Special Reserve, 30 km east of Moramanga. Furthermore, several differences and mistaken spellings occur in the literature and on-line resources. It must also be noted here that this portion of eastern Madagascar was previously administrated as the Province de Toamasina and in 2009 the national administration hierarchy was changed from provinces to regions, with the area now falling within the Alaotra-Mangoro Region. Many places throughout Madagascar have been renamed recently, and the system of administrative division presented by Viette (1991) has changed in the past years as well (see also Moravec 2022). Unfortunately, natural habitats in many localities have been rapidly disappearing over the past few years. Some of the unprotected areas near Moramanga, once full of tiger beetle species including those described as new for science, were totally destroyed by fire between 2001 and 2006 (see Moravec 2010, 2022, Moravec & VybÍral 2018); M. Trýzna and J. VybÍral pers. com. Severe fires also destroyed other parts of strictly preserved areas throughout Madagascar quite recently (e. g. Vyawahare 2020 and Andrianambinina et al. 2025). Fortunately, the Analamazaotra National Park remains one of the best protected areas. For the protected areas (map Fig. 20), phytogeography, ecosystems and biotopes see Goodman et al. (2018) and Goodman (2022). It is noteworthy that according to the coordinates written by the collector on the locality label, the male holotype of the new species was caught outside of the national park, somewhat southward from the NR 2, as obvious from the map Fig. 19. Nevertheless, as the national park is written on the locality label, we may speculate that the coordinates might have been written erroneously. We were unable to receive exact data on the habitats of the new species from the two collectors, yet the adult specimens were almost certainly caught on trunks of trees in the evergreen Analamazaotra forest. Adults and larvae of all species of the genus are strictly silvicolous and arboreal, confined to trees of all types of forest (see Emden (1935), Vadon (1935), Jeannel (1946 a, b), Rivalier (1970) Putchkov & Dolin (2005) and Moravec 2007).
